draft.title: Back emf in motors
card: A motor coil spins in a magnetic field. Its flux keeps changing, so it also acts as a generator and induces an emf in itself.
By Lenz's law, this induced emf opposes the change that causes it. It acts against the supply voltage, so it is called the back emf.
Back emf grows as the coil spins faster. The net voltage across the coil is the supply voltage minus the back emf. Current = net voltage ÷ coil resistance.
At the instant of starting, the coil is not moving, so there is no back emf. The net voltage is largest and so is the current. As the motor speeds up, the back emf rises and the current falls.
draft.remember: Faster spinning means more back emf, so less net voltage and less current.

a.q: A motor is switched on and its coil begins to spin faster. What happens to the back emf and the current drawn?
opts: Back emf rises and current falls
Back emf rises and current rises
Back emf falls and current falls
Back emf falls and current rises
a.why: A faster coil changes its flux more quickly, so the back emf rises. This cuts the net voltage across the coil, so the current falls. Current does not rise with speed, because the back emf opposes the supply.
a.clue: Net voltage is supply minus back emf.

b.q: A drill in Tom's workshop jams, and its coil stops spinning while it is still switched on. What happens to the current in the coil?
opts: It rises sharply, because the back emf drops to zero
It falls, because the coil is no longer moving
It stays the same, because the supply voltage is fixed
It falls, because the back emf rises as the coil stops
b.why: A stopped coil has no changing flux, so the back emf falls to zero. The net voltage across the coil is then at its largest, so the current is very high and can overheat the coil. The supply voltage is fixed, but the net voltage is not.
b.clue: Think about the instant a motor starts, when the coil is still.

a.best: Back emf rises and current falls

b.best: It rises sharply, because the back emf drops to zero
